entries:
From Middle High German künnen, kunnen, from Old High German kunnan, from Proto-West Germanic *kunnan, from Proto-Germanic *kunnaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃- (“to know”).
The umlauted ö in the infinitive and plural present—as well as the umlaut in the other modal verbs mögen (“to like”), müssen (“to have to”), and dürfen (“to be allowed to”)—is unexpected from an historical point of view. This umlaut first appeared in Middle High German and while a number of explanations have been proposed it is best interpreted as a transcategorial plural marker, that is to say the umlauted vowels are taken as a sign of plurality just as in nouns like Mutter–Mütter, Sohn–Söhne, Gans–Gänse, Haus–Häuser.
senses: to be able (to do or be something), to have the possibility of, can.

entries:
From a merger of:
* Middle High German riuwen (strong declension), from Old High German riuwan, hriuwan, from Proto-West Germanic *hreuwan, from Proto-Germanic *hrewwaną; and
* Middle High German riuwen (weak declension), itself a merger from Old High German riuwēn, from Proto-West Germanic *hriuwjan, from Proto-Germanic *hriuwjan; and Old High German riuwōn, hriuwōn, from Proto-West Germanic *hreuwōn, from *hreuwu (“regret, penance”).
Both paths derive from the same origin. Cognates include Dutch rouwen, English rue, Old Norse hryggva.
senses: to regret, to be sorry (for), to rue
